metadata.title: Computer Use: Demo to Production.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: what actually changes when you take a computer-use agent from a working demo to production? Lands the carry-out that production means every screenshot made leaner and every action logged, not the demo just running longer.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (a 20-step task burns ~40,000 screenshot tokens unoptimized; resize+prune cuts that 70-80%)

beats.narration_text: Hola — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here's the question I put to Claude: What actually changes between a demo and a system you can trust?

shot.new_visual_element: The composer types the reel's question, send button arms, running indicator follows

props.command: What actually changes between a demo and a system you can trust?

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a working computer-use demo is production-ready if you just let it run longer. It isn't — the real fix is leaner. So what actually changes between a demo and a system you can trust?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types the naive framing, hesitates on the wrong word, corrects it, lands the real question

props.text:
Going to production
just means running it
longer, right?

beats.narration_text: The naive computer-use loop: take a screenshot, send the full image to Claude, get an action, repeat. Screenshots are not free — a full-resolution screenshot costs around twelve hundred tokens. The natural assumption is that a working demo just runs longer once it's in production. It doesn't scale for free: a ten-step loop already spends twelve thousand tokens on screenshots before Claude does anything.

shot.new_visual_element: The naive loop (screenshot -> Claude -> action -> repeat) with a token counter climbing beside it toward twelve thousand

production_viz.label: The loop, and its running bill
production_viz.mechanic: Four boxes in a cycle on cream: 'screenshot' -> 'send to Claude' -> 'get an action' -> 'repeat', arrows looping back to the first. Beside the cycle, a token counter climbs step by step: ~1,200 tokens per screenshot, ticking up to 12,000 across ten loops, in terracotta once it crosses the naive-assumption line.

beats.narration_text: Here's the concrete case. A twenty-step task, no changes made, burns something like forty thousand tokens on screenshots alone — before a single action token is spent. That's the demo's real bill, and it only gets worse as the task gets longer.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - a bar building toward ~40,000 screenshot tokens against a 20-step task, action tokens still at zero beside it

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - the unoptimized bill
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A single vertical bar labelled '20-STEP TASK' grows upward in terracotta to a line marked '~40,000 screenshot tokens'. Beside it, a second, flat bar labelled 'action tokens spent' stays at zero. THIS EXACT BAR PAIR RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: The production version makes seven changes to that loop. Resize every screenshot to about fifteen sixty-eight pixels wide — the size Claude's vision already works best at. Drop screenshots older than the last few steps. Batch tool calls. Cache the system prompt. Compact the history server-side. Run actions in a sandbox. And record every action as a structured trajectory event.

shot.new_visual_element: Seven changes listed down a card, six bracketed as cost changes, the seventh (record) set apart

production_viz.label: Seven changes
production_viz.mechanic: A card on cream lists seven short lines in sequence: 'resize to ~1568px', 'prune old screenshots', 'batch tool calls', 'cache system prompt', 'compact server-side', 'sandbox execution' — a bracket beside the first six labelled 'shrinks the bill' in ink — then a seventh line, 'record every action', set apart below a thin rule, unlabelled by the bracket.

beats.narration_text: Back to that twenty-step task: resize and prune alone cut the screenshot bill seventy to eighty percent, because the savings compound rather than add. But the seventh change, recording, isn't about cost — a logged run proves what the agent did, not that it did the right thing, and a run with no log doesn't mean nothing went wrong. It means you can't tell.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the same bar cut down 70-80%; beside it, two log cards, one checked 'proves WHAT happened', one struck 'not WHETHER it was right'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - cut down, and the second question
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 BAR RETURNS, identical, then shrinks to a shorter bar marked '~40,000 -> ~10,000' with a check. Beside it, two small cards appear: one reading 'a log proves WHAT happened', checked in teal; the other reading 'not WHETHER it was right', struck through in terracotta. A third line beneath, unbracketed: 'no log doesn't mean nothing went wrong — it means you can't tell.'

beats.narration_text: Production isn't the demo running longer — it's every screenshot made leaner and every action logged, so the cost holds up and so does the record.

props.quote: Production isn't the demo running longer — it's every screenshot made leaner and every action logged, so the cost holds up and so does the record.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Design a trajectory logging schema for a computer-use agent: action type, target element, screenshot hash before and after, confidence score, and whether human confirmation was requested. Then ask: what else does the log need to make oversight meaningful, not just nominal? Liam, in for Bear.
